title: Cross-Validation, Grid Search and Randomized Search
abstract:
How hyperparameters are actually chosen. This document covers the three-way split
and why the test set must never be used for selection, $k$-fold cross-validation
and its variants, Grid Search CV and Randomized Search CV with the two flowcharts
from the notes, the mathematical reason random search beats grid search in more
than a couple of dimensions, nested cross-validation for an unbiased estimate,
and the pipeline discipline that stops the whole procedure from leaking.

blocks.t: The ML Flow
From the notes

Raw data $\rightarrow$ Train-Test Split (80–20) $\rightarrow$
Training data $\rightarrow$ Cross Validation (inside training)
$\rightarrow$ Hyperparameter tuning $\rightarrow$
Best model selected $\rightarrow$ Final Eval using Test data
From the notes: the three datasets

items: Training data — data used to teach the model.

Validation data — part of training data. Acts as a
 practice test before the exam. Roughly 10% validation, 90%
 training.

We train several models and evaluate the best on the validation
 set.

We don't use test data to select the model, as indirectly we
 would train on the test data.

As the model has not seen validation data, we hyperparameter tune
 using it, not the train data.

blocks.cap:
The flow and the notes that go with it. The single most important line
 is the one in red: the test set is not used for selection.

blocks.t: Why using the test set for selection inflates your score

Suppose you evaluate $G$ candidate configurations on the same test set. Each
observed score is $\text{true} + \text{noise}$, and you report the
maximum. The expected maximum of $G$ noisy estimates exceeds the true best
by roughly
\sigma\sqrt{2\ln G},

where $\sigma$ is the standard error of a single estimate. With $\sigma=0.02$ and
$G=100$ that is about $+0.06$ — six accuracy points of pure selection bias.

That is the formal content of "indirectly we would train on the test
data". The test set is a single-use instrument.
$k$-Fold Cross-Validation

blocks.cap:
Left: each fold takes a turn as validation. Right: why it matters —
 a single split's score varies wildly with the random seed, while the $k$-fold
 average is stable.

blocks.t: Why not just one validation split

A single 90/10 split gives one estimate from one arbitrary partition. Its
variance is large — often several accuracy points — so a model can look better
than a rival purely by seed. $k$-fold uses every row for validation exactly
once and averages, cutting the variance of the estimate by roughly $\sqrt{k}$ and
using all the data for training in some fold.

rows: Preserves the class ratio in every fold — the default for classification, and essential when imbalanced
Keeps all rows of a group (a customer, a patient) in the same fold. Prevents leakage through near-duplicates
Train on the past, validate on the future. Mandatory for temporal data (Topic 22)
$k=n$. Nearly unbiased but high variance and $n$ fits
Repeat $k$-fold with different partitions and average

From the notes

head: Grid Search CV
Randomized Search CV
rows: Tries all possible combinations of hyperparameters you give

Randomly samples combinations from the parameter space you give.
 Control randomness $=$ n_iter

blocks.cap: The two procedures, and the geometric reason random search wins.

blocks.t: Why random search beats grid search

Cost. A grid over $p$ parameters with $v$ values each is $v^p$
combinations — exponential. Four parameters with five values each is 625 fits,
times $k$ folds. Random search costs exactly n_iter fits, chosen by you.

Coverage. This is the deeper reason (Bergstra & Bengio, 2012). In
practice only one or two hyperparameters matter much. A $5\times5$ grid spends 25
trials but explores only 5 distinct values of the important parameter —
the other 20 trials merely repeat those five while varying something irrelevant.
Random search with 25 trials explores 25 distinct values of every
parameter.

Probability. If the best 5% of the space is acceptable, $N$ random
trials find it with probability $1-0.95^{N}$: 60 trials give 95% confidence,
independently of the number of dimensions.
Which to use

Grid search when you have one or two parameters and a small, meaningful set of
candidate values. Random search for anything larger, and for continuous
parameters where a grid is arbitrary. Optuna (Topic 81) improves on both by
learning from the trials so far rather than sampling blindly.
Nested Cross-Validation
The subtlety that catches almost everyone

After GridSearchCV, best_score_ is the CV score of the
selected configuration — and it was selected because it scored
highest. It is therefore optimistically biased by exactly the
$\sigma\sqrt{2\ln G}$ argument above. Reporting it as your model's performance
repeats the mistake the test set was meant to prevent, one level down.

Nested CV fixes it: an inner loop selects hyperparameters, an outer loop
evaluates the whole selection procedure on data the inner loop never saw.

rows: Estimates the performance of "tune, then fit"

blocks.t:
Cost: $k_{\text{out}}\times k_{\text{in}}\times G$ fits. In practice, a held-out
test set touched once (the notes' flow) achieves the same thing far more cheaply
— which is why nested CV is reserved for small datasets and for papers.
Pipelines Are Not Optional Here
Preprocessing must be inside the CV loop

Everything from Topic 17 applies with force. If you scale, impute or select
features on the full training set and then cross-validate, every validation
fold has already influenced the transformation. The reported score is optimistic
— catastrophically so for feature selection.

Pass a Pipeline to GridSearchCV and scikit-learn refits every
transformer on each fold's training portion. The step__param syntax then
lets you tune preprocessing choices alongside model hyperparameters.
Code

import numpy as np, time, warnings
from scipy.stats import loguniform, randint
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif
from sklearn.model_selection import (train_test_split, cross_val_score, KFold,
                                     StratifiedKFold, GroupKFold, TimeSeriesSplit,
                                     GridSearchCV, RandomizedSearchCV, cross_validate)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 2000
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 10))
y = (1.6*X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] - .7*X[:, 2] + .5*X[:, 0]*X[:, 1]
     + rng.normal(0, 1.2, n) > 0).astype(int)

# STEP 1 of the flow: train-test split (80-20). The test set is now SEALED.
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.2,
                                          stratify=y, random_state=0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. ONE SPLIT IS A LOTTERY
# =====================================================================
singles = []
for s in range(30):
    a, b, c, d = train_test_split(X_tr, y_tr, test_size=.2, random_state=s)
    singles.append(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=0,
                                          n_jobs=-1).fit(a, c).score(b, d))
cvs = [cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=0,
                                              n_jobs=-1),
                       X_tr, y_tr, cv=KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=s),
                       n_jobs=-1).mean() for s in range(8)]
print(f"single 80/20 split : mean {np.mean(singles):.4f}  sd {np.std(singles):.4f}  "
      f"range {np.ptp(singles):.4f}")
print(f"5-fold CV          : mean {np.mean(cvs):.4f}  sd {np.std(cvs):.4f}  "
      f"range {np.ptp(cvs):.4f}")
# The single split's answer swings by several points on the seed alone.

# =====================================================================
# 2. THE CV VARIANTS
# =====================================================================
y_imb = (rng.random(len(y_tr)) < .06).astype(int)          # 6% positive
print(f"\nimbalanced data, positive rate {y_imb.mean():.3f}")
for name, cv in [("KFold", KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)),
                 ("StratifiedKFold", StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0))]:
    rates = [y_imb[te].mean() for _, te in cv.split(X_tr, y_imb)]
    print(f"  {name:16s} fold positive rates: {np.round(rates, 3)}")
# Plain KFold can produce a fold with almost no positives. Stratified cannot.

groups = rng.integers(0, 200, len(X_tr))
gk = GroupKFold(5)
print(f"\nGroupKFold: no group spans folds: "
      f"{all(len(set(groups[tr]) & set(groups[te])) == 0 for tr, te in gk.split(X_tr, y_tr, groups))}")

ts = TimeSeriesSplit(5)
print("TimeSeriesSplit (train always precedes validation):")
for tr, te in list(ts.split(X_tr))[:3]:
    print(f"  train rows 0..{tr.max():4d}   validate {te.min()}..{te.max()}")

# =====================================================================
# 3. GRID SEARCH CV -- all possible combinations
# =====================================================================
grid = {"n_estimators":      [100, 300],
        "max_features":      ["sqrt", "log2", 0.5],
        "max_depth":         [None, 8, 16],
        "min_samples_leaf":  [1, 4, 8]}
n_comb = np.prod([len(v) for v in grid.values()])
print(f"\ngrid: {n_comb} combinations x 5 folds = {n_comb*5} fits")

t0 = time.perf_counter()
gs = GridSearchCV(RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0, n_jobs=-1),
                  grid, cv=5, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
t_grid = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"grid search: {t_grid:.1f}s   best cv {gs.best_score_:.4f}")
print(f"  {gs.best_params_}")

# =====================================================================
# 4. RANDOMIZED SEARCH CV -- n_iter controls the randomness
# =====================================================================
dist = {"n_estimators":     randint(50, 600),
        "max_features":     loguniform(0.05, 1.0),        # CONTINUOUS
        "max_depth":        [None] + list(range(4, 40, 2)),
        "min_samples_leaf": randint(1, 20)}
t0 = time.perf_counter()
rs = RandomizedSearchCV(RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0, n_jobs=-1),
                        dist, n_iter=30, cv=5, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
t_rand = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"\nrandom search (n_iter=30): {t_rand:.1f}s   best cv {rs.best_score_:.4f}")
print(f"  {rs.best_params_}")
print(f"random search used {30/n_comb:.0%} of the fits and scored "
      f"{rs.best_score_ - gs.best_score_:+.4f} relative to the grid")

# WHY: coverage of the IMPORTANT parameter
print(f"\ndistinct max_features values explored:")
print(f"  grid  : {len(set(str(p['max_features']) for p in gs.cv_results_['params']))}")
print(f"  random: {len(set(round(p['max_features'], 4) for p in rs.cv_results_['params']))}")
# The grid repeats 3 values 18 times each; random search tries 30 distinct ones.

# THE PROBABILITY ARGUMENT
print(f"\n{'n_iter':>7s} {'P(hit the top 5%)':>18s}")
for N in [10, 30, 60, 100]:
    print(f"{N:7d} {1 - 0.95**N:18.3f}")
# 60 random trials find the top 5% with 95% confidence, in ANY dimension.

# =====================================================================
# 5. best_score_ IS OPTIMISTICALLY BIASED
# =====================================================================
print(f"\ngs.best_score_ (used for SELECTION): {gs.best_score_:.4f}")
print(f"score on the sealed test set       : {gs.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")
print(f"optimism: {gs.best_score_ - gs.score(X_te, y_te):+.4f}")

sigma = gs.cv_results_["std_test_score"][gs.best_index_] / np.sqrt(5)
print(f"expected selection bias ~ sigma*sqrt(2 ln G) = "
      f"{sigma*np.sqrt(2*np.log(n_comb)):.4f}")

# NESTED CV -- an unbiased estimate of the whole tune-then-fit procedure
inner = GridSearchCV(RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0, n_jobs=-1),
                     {"max_features": ["sqrt", "log2", 0.5],
                      "min_samples_leaf": [1, 4, 8]},
                     cv=3, n_jobs=-1)
nested = cross_val_score(inner, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5, n_jobs=-1)
print(f"\nnested CV estimate: {nested.mean():.4f} +/- {nested.std():.4f}")
print(f"(non-nested best_score_ was {gs.best_score_:.4f} -- optimistic)")

# =====================================================================
# 6. PREPROCESSING MUST BE INSIDE THE CV LOOP
# =====================================================================
Xn = rng.normal(0, 1, (200, 2000))                   # PURE NOISE
yn = rng.integers(0, 2, 200)

sel = SelectKBest(f_classif, k=20).fit(Xn, yn)       # used ALL the labels
leaky = cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=0),
                        sel.transform(Xn), yn, cv=5).mean()
clean = cross_val_score(Pipeline([("sel", SelectKBest(f_classif, k=20)),
                                  ("clf", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100,
                                                                 random_state=0))]),
                        Xn, yn, cv=5).mean()
print(f"\non PURE NOISE:")
print(f"  selection outside CV: {leaky:.3f}   <- an artefact")
print(f"  selection inside a Pipeline: {clean:.3f}   <- correct")

# =====================================================================
# 7. TUNING PREPROCESSING AND MODEL TOGETHER
# =====================================================================
X_miss = X_tr.copy()
X_miss[rng.random(X_miss.shape) < .08] = np.nan

pipe = Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer()),
                 ("sc",  StandardScaler()),
                 ("sel", SelectKBest(f_classif)),
                 ("clf", SVC())])
gs2 = GridSearchCV(pipe, {
    "imp__strategy": ["mean", "median"],
    "sc__with_std":  [True, False],
    "sel__k":        [5, 8, 10],
    "clf__C":        [0.1, 1, 10],
    "clf__gamma":    ["scale", 0.1],
}, cv=5, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_miss, y_tr)
print(f"\nbest across preprocessing AND model: {gs2.best_params_}")
print(f"cv {gs2.best_score_:.4f}")
# The imputation strategy is now a tuned hyperparameter, chosen with evidence.

# =====================================================================
# 8. INSPECTING THE RESULTS, AND THE 1-SE RULE
# =====================================================================
import pandas as pd
res = pd.DataFrame(gs.cv_results_)[
    ["mean_test_score", "std_test_score", "mean_fit_time", "params"]
].sort_values("mean_test_score", ascending=False)
print("\ntop 5 configurations:")
for _, r in res.head(5).iterrows():
    print(f"  {r.mean_test_score:.4f} +/- {r.std_test_score:.4f}  "
          f"({r.mean_fit_time:.2f}s)  {r.params}")

best = res.mean_test_score.iloc[0]
se = res.std_test_score.iloc[0] / np.sqrt(5)
within = res[res.mean_test_score >= best - se]
print(f"\n{len(within)} configurations are within one standard error of the best")
simplest = within.sort_values("mean_fit_time").iloc[0]
print(f"the cheapest of them: {simplest.mean_test_score:.4f}  {simplest.params}")
# The '1-SE rule': among statistically indistinguishable models, take the
# simplest. It generalises better and costs less to serve.

# Multiple metrics at once:
out = cross_validate(gs.best_estimator_, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5,
                     scoring=["accuracy", "roc_auc", "f1"], n_jobs=-1)
for k in ["test_accuracy", "test_roc_auc", "test_f1"]:
    print(f"{k:16s} {out[k].mean():.4f} +/- {out[k].std():.4f}")

# FINAL STEP OF THE FLOW: evaluate ONCE on the sealed test set
print(f"\nFINAL test score: {gs.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")
Worked Examples
5-fold cross-validation and the cost of a grid
Step 1 – fold scores. Accuracy on the five held-out folds: $[0.82,\;0.85,\;0.80,\;0.88,\;0.84]$.
Report it as $0.838 \pm 0.030$. The spread tells you whether a difference between two models is meaningful.
Step 2 – the cost of a grid. Grid over $C \in \{0.1,1,10\}$ and max_depth $\in \{3,5,7,9\}$:
3 \times 4 = 12 \text{ combinations}, \qquad 12 \times 5 \text{ folds} = 60 \text{ model fits}
Step 3 – randomised search. Sampling 5 combinations instead of 12 costs $5\times 5 = 25$ fits and often finds a near-best setting.

Step 4 – nested CV. Tuning and evaluating on the same folds biases the score upward. The correct structure is an outer loop for evaluation and an inner loop for the grid search. Scikit-learn's GridSearchCV inside cross_val_score does this.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Why do you need a validation set when you already have a test set?

Because selecting on the test set makes the test set part of training. After $G$
comparisons the best observed score exceeds the truth by roughly
$\sigma\sqrt{2\ln G}$ — with 100 candidates and a 2% standard error, six points
of pure optimism. Validation absorbs the selection; test stays a clean, single-use
estimate.
Q. Why $k$-fold rather than one validation split?

A single split gives one estimate from one arbitrary partition, and its variance
is large enough that a model can appear better than a rival purely by seed.
$k$-fold validates on every row exactly once and averages, reducing the variance
by roughly $\sqrt{k}$.
Q. Grid search or randomized search?

Grid for one or two parameters with a small set of meaningful values. Random for
anything larger, and for continuous parameters. Random search costs exactly what
you budget, and it explores far more distinct values of whichever parameter
actually matters.
Q. Why does random search beat grid search in high dimensions?

Because usually only one or two hyperparameters matter, and a grid wastes trials
repeating the same few values of the important one while varying irrelevant ones.
Twenty-five grid points give five distinct values of each axis; twenty-five random
points give twenty-five.
Q. Can you report best_score_ as your model's performance?

No. It is the score of the configuration chosen because it scored highest,
so it carries the same selection bias. Report the score on a held-out test set
touched once, or use nested cross-validation.
Q. What breaks if you scale before cross-validating?

The scaler's statistics were computed using every fold, including the ones held
out, so each validation fold is contaminated and the CV estimate is optimistic.
For feature selection the effect is dramatic — selecting the top 20 of 2000
pure-noise features outside the loop yields apparently good accuracy on data with
no signal.
Q. What is the one-standard-error rule?

Among configurations whose CV score is within one standard error of the best, take
the simplest. Those models are statistically indistinguishable, and the simpler
one generalises better and is cheaper to serve.
